title: One ticket, one run

story: You assign RH-1234 to Nova and go get coffee. The Jira poll notices the ticket within a minute and starts a run. Nova claims a VM and starts reading the code.

Back at your desk you are not sure anything happened, so you type /nova RH-1234 in Slack. Then the poll runs again, because it runs every minute and RH-1234 is still assigned to Nova. That is three requests to start work on one ticket in two minutes, and the poll will keep asking every minute. If each request starts its own run, we pay for several VMs and get several agents pushing to the same branch.
hook.question: How do we make sure one ticket only ever gets one run, no matter how many times someone asks?

lines.say: On the left are three requests to start work on the same ticket: the Jira poll, you typing slash nova in Slack, and the poll again one minute later, because the ticket is still assigned to Nova.
In the middle is Temporal. Every start goes through Temporal, and Temporal creates the run that actually does the work.
Every run needs a name, called its workflow ID. Let's start with the lazy choice: a random name each time.

cue.caption: workflow ID: the name of a run

lines.say: The poll finds RH-1234 and asks Temporal for a run. Temporal has never seen this random name, so it starts Run 1.
Run 1 needs a machine. Nova may use only three machines at once, and each of those places is called a VM slot. Run 1 takes one of them.

cue.caption: VM slot: one of the 3 machines Nova may use

lines.say: A minute later you type slash nova RH-1234. Another random name, so Temporal starts Run 2.
Then the poll runs again a minute later. It finds the same ticket, asks again, and Run 3 starts.
Look at the VM slots: all three are now busy with the same ticket.
Nothing is broken here. Temporal did exactly what it was asked. The problem is that a random name tells Temporal nothing about what the run is for, so it cannot know these three are the same job.

cue.caption: random names: every trigger makes a new run

check.q: With random workflow IDs, the Jira poll finds RH-1234 every minute for ten minutes. How many runs start?

options.text: One, because it is the same ticket
options.why: Temporal only knows the name you give it. Ten random names look like ten different jobs.
Each poll asks for a run with a new random name, so each one starts. (In practice the VM slots would run out first, and the extra runs would wait.)
Any string is a valid workflow ID. Temporal does not judge the name, it only refuses a second open run with the same one.

chapters.title: Name the run after the ticket

lines.say: Here is the fix. Instead of a random name, we name the run after the thing it works on: the agent, a colon, and the ticket key. So this run is called nova colon RH-1234.

cue.caption: the ID is the thing: nova:RH-1234

lines.say: Temporal has one firm rule about names: only one open run may hold a given workflow ID at a time. Now that the name means something, that rule works for us.
The poll asks first. No open run has this name, so Temporal starts it.

Now your Slack command asks for a run with the same name. Temporal sees that nova colon RH-1234 is already open. What should happen next is up to us, and the setting that decides it is called the conflict policy.

cue.caption: conflict policy: what a second start does

lines.say: The default policy is called fail. The second start throws an error that says the workflow is already started. That is safe, because there is still only one run, but the person in Slack just sees an error.

cue.caption: FAIL, the default: the second start gets an error

lines.say: The policy we use is called use existing. The second start does not create anything. Instead it gets back a handle, an object that points to the run that is already working, so Slack can reply with a link to it.
The poll's next request does the same and joins too. Three requests, one run, one VM. The rest of the platform never has to ask whether a duplicate is possible, because the name rules it out.

check.q: The run nova:RH-1234 is working, and someone types /nova RH-1234. The conflict policy is USE_EXISTING. What does the Slack command get back?

options.text: A handle to the run that is already working
options.why: USE_EXISTING joins the open run instead of starting a new one, so Slack can link to it.

options.text: An error saying the run already exists
options.why: That is the default policy, FAIL. USE_EXISTING is there exactly to avoid that error.

options.text: A fresh run that replaces the old one
options.why: That would be TERMINATE_EXISTING, which throws away the work in progress. We never use it.

chapters.title: The trap, and when a name is free again

lines.say: There is a third policy, and it looks tempting: terminate existing. It kills the open run and starts a fresh one.
Picture Nova seventy percent through the ticket. Someone types slash nova again, just to check. With terminate existing, that innocent check throws away everything Nova has done.

cue.caption: TERMINATE_EXISTING: a second trigger kills real work

lines.say: So a second trigger should never be able to destroy work. That is why we join and never terminate.
One last detail. The rule only covers open runs. When a run finishes, its name is free again.
So if RH-1234's run ends today, and the ticket is assigned to Nova again next week, the poll starts a brand new run with the same name. That is what we want: a fresh run with a fresh VM.
Remember this: name each run after the thing it works on, and let a second start join the open run. Then one ticket can only ever have one run.

cue.caption: name the run after the thing · join, never terminate

play.intro: Fire triggers at Temporal and watch what each choice of name and conflict policy does to your runs, your VMs and your bill. Guess first, then press Run.

tasks.text: With random IDs, how many runs do three triggers make?
With the ticket as the ID and the default policy, what does the person in Slack see?
Switch to TERMINATE_EXISTING while Nova is 70% done, then type /nova. What happened to the work?
Finish the run, then reassign the ticket. Why does a new run start with the same name?

p: A workflow ID is the name of a run. You choose it when you start the run, and Temporal enforces one rule about it: in a namespace (a separate space in Temporal for one group of workflows; ours is called ai-agents), only one open run may hold a given ID at a time. A random ID throws that rule away, because no two random names are ever equal. So we name every run after the thing it works on, prefixed with the agent: nova:RH-1234 for a ticket, cifix:fcp:3fa91c for the CI fixer working on one broken main branch, upgrade:fcp:pr-812 for one dependency PR.
In our code every run starts through one small function, startRun, so nobody can forget the rule. The Jira poll, the Slack app and the schedules all call it.

notes.text: The name is the agent plus the thing, for example nova:RH-1234. Two triggers for the same ticket produce the same name.
Each agent has its own queue, so a storm of one kind of work cannot take every worker. The next lesson is about queues.
If a run with this name is already open, return a handle to it instead of starting a second one.

read.h: Three answers to a second start
p: When a start arrives for a name that already has an open run, the conflict policy decides what happens. FAIL is the default: the start throws WorkflowExecutionAlreadyStartedError, which is safe but makes every caller handle an error. USE_EXISTING returns a handle to the open run, so the caller can show a link or wait for the result. TERMINATE_EXISTING kills the open run and starts again, which means any repeated trigger can destroy work in progress. We use USE_EXISTING everywhere and never TERMINATE_EXISTING.
You can see the first two side by side on your laptop. The code below shows both in a few lines, and the lab lets you run them yourself.

notes.text: The second start with USE_EXISTING gets a handle to the same run.
Without a policy you get the default, FAIL, and this start throws.

read.see:
same run: true
default policy: WorkflowExecutionAlreadyStartedError

p: The one-run-per-name rule only looks at runs that are still open. Once a run completes, fails or is cancelled, its name is free, and the next start creates a new run with the same ID. For tickets that is what we want: a ticket that Nova handed back after waiting too long, and that is assigned to Nova again, gets a fresh run, with a fresh VM and a clean history.

Temporal can also remember closed names, through a second setting called the reuse policy. Its default, ALLOW_DUPLICATE, is the behaviour described above. REJECT_DUPLICATE refuses a name that was used before, for as long as Temporal keeps the old run's history.

Sometimes the second trigger carries information the run needs. When main breaks, every red build is another piece of evidence about the same problem. For that case Temporal has signalWithStart: one call that sends a signal (a message) to the open run, or starts the run and then delivers the signal to it. Either way the message arrives, and there is still only one run.

Our CI fixer uses signalWithStart together with REJECT_DUPLICATE. If the same root cause comes back after its run has closed, the fixer probably did not fix it, so a person should look instead of starting the same fix again. You will build this in the lesson about the CI fixer's triggers.

lab.title: One ticket, one run
needs: About 150 MB of disk for the Temporal packages
lab.goal: Make every trigger for the same ticket land in one Temporal run, by naming the run after the ticket and joining the run that is already open.

guess.q: The Jira poll, Slack /nova and a Jira comment all ask Nova to work on the same ticket within one minute. The run's ID is nova:RH-1234 and you did not set a conflict policy. What happens?

options.text: Three runs start, and Nova does the work three times.
options.why: Temporal never keeps two open runs with the same ID, so a fixed ID makes this impossible.

options.text: The first trigger starts the run, and the second and third get a WorkflowExecutionAlreadyStartedError.
options.why: That is Temporal's default: it refuses a second start while the run is open. USE_EXISTING turns that error into "here is the run that is already open".

options.text: The last trigger wins: it stops the first run and starts a new one.
options.why: That is TERMINATE_EXISTING, which you must ask for. It is never the default, and the platform never uses it, because it throws work away.

lab.build: Open start-run.mjs and change three options: workflowId becomes `${agent}:${thing}`, taskQueue becomes `ai-agents-${agent}`, and add workflowIdConflictPolicy: WorkflowIdConflictPolicy.USE_EXISTING. Run node clean.mjs && node triggers.mjs: all three triggers now show the ID nova:RH-1234 with the same run, and the summary says 3 triggers for RH-1234 → 1 run. Approve that run to finish the story, temporal workflow signal --workflow-id nova:RH-1234 --name approve --input '"Dana"', and watch the worker terminal say "Dana approved RH-1234". Finish with ./academy check while the dev server is still running.
lab.fix: Someone wanted the newest trigger to win, so they changed one word in startRun. Today Nova worked on a ticket for 40 minutes, then Sean typed /nova in Slack to ask how it was going, and Nova started again from zero. Run node clean.mjs && node triggers.mjs --fix to see two TERMINATED runs, then repair fix/start-run.mjs so a new trigger joins the open run.
explain: Why is the run's workflow ID nova:RH-1234 and not a random ID?
A second trigger arrives while the run is still open. What does each policy do: the default (FAIL), USE_EXISTING, and TERMINATE_EXISTING?
Why should the platform never use TERMINATE_EXISTING for an agent's run?
lab.done: Three triggers for one ticket show one run, ./academy check passes, and you stopped the worker and the dev server with Ctrl+C.

check.q: Your teammate suggests random UUIDs for workflow IDs "so they never collide". What goes wrong?

options.text: Nothing; collisions are the real danger
options.why: For us a collision is the point. Two triggers for one ticket should collide, so the second one joins instead of starting a duplicate.

options.text: Every trigger starts its own run, so one ticket can get several agents and VMs
options.why: Temporal only refuses a second open run with the same name. Random names are never the same, so nothing stops duplicates.

options.text: Temporal rejects UUIDs as workflow IDs
options.why: Any string works as an ID. The problem is what the name means, not its format.

check.q: Why do we never use TERMINATE_EXISTING?

options.why: Speed is not the issue. The issue is what it does to the run that is already working.

options.text: It is deprecated in the TypeScript SDK
options.why: It is a supported policy. It is simply the wrong behaviour for agent runs.

options.text: Any repeated trigger, even a harmless check, would kill the run in progress and throw away its work
options.why: Triggers repeat all the time (the poll runs every minute). A policy that lets them destroy work is a trap.

check.q: RH-1234's run finished yesterday. Today the ticket is assigned to Nova again. With the default reuse policy, what happens?

options.text: A new run starts with the same ID, nova:RH-1234
options.why: The one-run rule only covers open runs. A finished run frees its name.

options.text: The start joins yesterday's finished run
options.why: USE_EXISTING only joins runs that are still open. A finished run cannot be joined.

options.text: The start fails because the ID was used before
options.why: That would need REJECT_DUPLICATE. The default, ALLOW_DUPLICATE, lets the name be used again.

p: Every agent run in the platform starts through startRun, with the agent and the thing as its name: nova:RH-1234 for a ticket, cifix:fcp:<fingerprint> for one broken main branch. Only the orchestrator starts runs. A VM has no route to Temporal, so an agent can never start another agent.
The CI fixer builds on this lesson with signalWithStart and REJECT_DUPLICATE, so that a whole storm of red builds becomes one run, and a problem that comes back goes to a person.

tickets.why: startRun, the naming rule and USE_EXISTING are this lesson.
One CI-fixer run per root cause: signalWithStart plus REJECT_DUPLICATE.
A parked ticket that is assigned again gets a fresh run with the same name.

words.plain: The name of a run. Only one open run can have a given name at a time.
A run that has not finished yet: it is working, or waiting for something.
What a start does when a run with the same name is already open: fail, join it, or kill it.
Whether a name can be used again after its run has finished.
One call that sends a message to the open run, or starts the run and then sends the message.

videos.title: Temporal in 7 Minutes – the TL;DR Intro
videos.why: A quick refresher on what Temporal does, if runs and workflows still feel fuzzy.

review.q: Write the three options of startRun from memory: the ID, the task queue and the conflict policy.
A teammate wants TERMINATE_EXISTING so that "a re-trigger restarts cleanly". What do you answer?
review.a: Triggers repeat constantly, so any of them would kill work in progress. If a run must restart, that is a deliberate action (cancel, then start), not a side effect of a trigger.

review.q: Why does a ticket that Nova handed back that is assigned again get a new run, and when would you want REJECT_DUPLICATE instead?
review.a: Only open runs block a name, so a closed run frees it. REJECT_DUPLICATE fits when a repeat means something went wrong, like a broken-main root cause that comes back after its fix.

remember: Name each run after the thing it works on, and let a second start join the open run: one ticket, one run.
